description: Exercise can improve physical functioning in cancer patients. It can reduce the feelings of fatigue, depression, nausea and weakness that can arise during and after cancer treatment. The UCSF Core and More class includes Pilates-based mat exercises to work on core strength and stability. We use rollers, bands and body weight as tools to enhance range of motion, flexibility, balance and muscular strength. Our goal is for you to have fun and increase your ability to perform daily activities. This class is sponsored by the UCSF Cancer Resource Center. It is open to current UCSF cancer patients and survivors. Registration is required for this class. To participate, you must undergo a pre-screening with an exercise counselor. For more information, call (415) 502-5547. There may be a waitlist for this course.

description: QiGong is a traditional Chinese healing system, similar to Tai Chi. According to the NCCIH, "it involves using exercises to optimize energy within the body, mind, and spirit, with the goal of improving and maintaining health and well-being. QiGong has both psychological and physical components and involves the regulation of the mind, breath, and body's movement and posture." In clinical trials, it has been shown to improve balance in participants. This class focuses on improving health and well-being and is appropriate for people experiencing cancer and chronic conditions. The class accommodates people with movement restrictions or even chair-based practitioners. *UCSF cancer patients and their caregivers are welcome to attend this weekly free online class, held every Wednesday from 2:30 - 3:30 pm.

description: A multidisciplinary symposium bringing together researchers, clinicians, educators, pharmacologists, trainees, and experts across maternal and child health, precision medicine, translational science, and implementation science to advance safe, effective, and individualized pharmacotherapy for pregnant women, fetuses, and children. description: The original Gratitude in Action Webinar was first developed and introduced to the UC community in November 2023 as a part of the FSAP Wellness Webinar Series. We invite you now to join us for what has become our Annual November Gratitude Webinar for another opportunity to engage, re-engage, and learn more about developing your own personal practice of Mindful Gratitude. This webinar explores current research on gratitude, including its potential benefits for managing stress, our own wellbeing, and how we experience and respond to the world around us. Given the unique experiences and demands of the UC Community in mind, this webinar will focus on brief, practical approaches to gratitude that can be incorporated into everyday life. Whether you’re interested in returning to a gratitude practice you’ve used before, have tried gratitude practices in the past that didn’t quite work for you, or are simply curious about where to begin, this webinar will help you explore different approaches and identify what might be most useful and sustainable for you. As we head into the winter season, join us for an hour of your workday to step away from the usual demands, learn what the research tells us about gratitude, and experiment with a few ways of putting it into practice. During this webinar, participants will: • Learn about current research on gratitude and its potential benefits for well-being • Explore different approaches to incorporating gratitude into daily life • Identify common barriers to starting and maintaining a gratitude practice • Consider how technology, relationships, and the workplace can help support a practice • Experiment with several brief gratitude practices • Develop a personalized plan for incorporating gratitude in a way that feels realistic and sustainable Presenter Bio: Jessica Allanson, PhD, MA, is a licensed clinical psychologist with the Faculty and Staff Assistance Program at UCSF and runs the FSAP Post-Doctoral Fellowship Program. Dr. Allanson has chosen to specialize in recovery from substance use and workplace burnout, working primarily with those in high-intensity work settings and with high-achieving populations. She incorporates empirically-validated skill-based learning as well as industrial/organizational psychology strategies into her work with individual clients, teams, leaders, and learners. Dr. Allanson believes in the power of compassionate education and hopes to use her passion for sharing and teaching to support and empower those who are curious.

description: This event is in-person only, but open to all. To receive the calendar invite, email Julia Wu (Julia.Wu@ucsf.edu) Contemporary mindfulness programs have demonstrated benefits for health and well-being, yet their application within Indigenous communities requires attention to cultural context, historical trauma, and Indigenous ways of knowing. This presentation introduces IndigenousMIND, a community-engaged framework that integrates evidence-based mindfulness approaches with Indigenous cultural practices, including storytelling, ceremony, traditional arts, and relationships with land and community. Drawing on research and collaborations with Indigenous Nations, Dr. Proulx will discuss lessons learned in adapting mindfulness interventions, emerging findings related to stress and cardiovascular health, and opportunities for culturally grounded approaches to integrative health and healing. Jeffrey Proulx, PhD, is a Haudenosaunee (Six Nations) scholar, researcher, and educator whose work focuses on culturally grounded mindfulness interventions andhealth equity in underserved communities. He is adjunct faculty at Brown University, where he has held appointments in Psychiatry and Human Behavior, Behavioral and Social Sciences, and Contemplative Studies. He is also Vice President and co-founder of the Indigenous Mindfulness Coalition, an Indigenous-led nonprofit dedicated to supporting Indigenous well-being through contemplative practices, cultural revitalization, research, and community engagement. Dr. Proulx developed the IndigenousMIND framework, which brings together contemporary mindfulness approaches with Indigenous cultural practices, values, and ways of knowing. His research, supported by the National Institutes of Health and private foundations, explores the potential of culturally adapted mindfulness interventions to address stress, hypertension, intergenerational trauma, and other health disparities. He is also co-editor of Beyond White Mindfulness: Critical Perspectives on Racism, Well-Being, and Liberation (Routledge, 2022). The Osher Center for Integrative Health hosts monthly research seminars that are open to the research and clinical community at large. Seminars are held from September to June and are generally virtual. Presentations cover a wide range of topics relating to integrative health, many with a focus on integrative health equity. Research Seminars are organized by Ariana Thompson-Lastad, PhD and Joanne Qina’au, PhD, MA, E-YT750. Please contact Julia Wu (julia.wu@ucsf.edu) with any questions., powered by Localist, the Community Event Platform

description: Making Health Promotion Meaningful: Community-engaged Strategies for Reaching Diverse Priority Populations Presented by Simona C. Kwon, DrPH, MPH Simona C. Kwon, DrPH, MPH, is an associate professor in the Department of Population Health at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and serves as director of the NYU Center for the Study of Asian American Health. She is nationally recognized for her expertise in community-based participatory research (CBPR) and health equity initiatives aimed at reducing health disparities in immigrant and minority populations. Dr. Kwon’s research focuses on chronic disease prevention, cultural competency in healthcare, and the social determinants of health. She has led multiple NIH-funded projects addressing health issues in underserved communities, with a particular focus on Asian American populations. As a leader in public health, Dr. Kwon collaborates with community-based organizations to design and implement culturally tailored interventions. Her work highlights the importance of building trust and partnerships between healthcare systems and the communities they serve. She has published extensively on CBPR methodologies and health equity frameworks. Dr. Kwon is committed to advancing inclusive and equitable approaches to improving health outcomes across diverse populations. Learning Objectives: At the end of this activity, learners will be able to: Apply key principles of social marketing and cultural adaptation that can inform efforts to close gaps between current and ideal practice in health promotion and disease prevention for reaching priority populations. Describe how community engagement, participatory approaches, and cultural relevance can support more whole-person, integrated care through clinical practice, research, and education for diverse priority populations. Identify broad strategies for adapting evidence-based health programs to improve relevance, implementation, and sustainability in priority communities, with the goal of improving health outcomes.
